slides.title: Why 1e-8 disappears in FP16
slides.lede: A 16-bit type is not automatically a safe training type. The exponent budget decides whether a small gradient is representable at all.
beats: FP16: 1 sign + 5 exponent + 10 fraction bits.
The smallest positive FP16 subnormal is about 5.96e-8, so 1e-8 rounds to zero.
Once a gradient becomes exactly zero, no later optimizer step can recover that signal.
slides.check: Predict what happens to 1e-7, 1e-8, and 1e-9 before running the torch expression from the lecture.

slides.title: BF16 spends its bits on range
slides.lede: BF16 keeps FP32's eight exponent bits and reduces the fraction to seven bits. It preserves dynamic range, not FP32-level resolution.
beats: FP32: 1 / 8 / 23 sign, exponent, fraction bits.
BF16 represents 1e-8 as nonzero, but nearby values are quantized more coarsely than in FP16.
slides.check: Range and precision are different axes: ask first whether a value survives, then how accurately it is rounded.

slides.title: Expose a hidden sub-dimension, transform it, then join
slides.lede: The lecture uses rearrange to split total_hidden into heads × hidden1, einsum to apply w: hidden1 → hidden2 inside every head, then rearrange to join the heads again.
beats: Input x has shape [sequence, total_hidden=8], where 8 = 2 heads × hidden1=4.
Pattern ... (heads hidden1) -> ... heads hidden1 makes hidden1 independently addressable; einsum with w[4,3] changes it to hidden2=3.
Pattern ... heads hidden2 -> ... (heads hidden2) joins the heads, producing total_hidden=6.
slides.check: Rearrange itself preserves values. The intervening einsum, not rearrange, is what changes each head from width 4 to width 3.
slides.code: x = rearrange(x, '... (heads hidden1) -> ... heads hidden1', heads=2); x = einsum(x, w, '... hidden1, hidden1 hidden2 -> ... hidden2'); x = rearrange(x, '... heads hidden2 -> ... (heads hidden2)')

slides.title: One plot, two bottlenecks
slides.lede: For H100 BF16, the roofline predicts attainable throughput as the lower of 3.35 TB/s times arithmetic intensity and 989.5 TFLOP/s peak compute.
beats: Both axes are logarithmic; arithmetic intensity I is useful work divided by bytes moved.
The H100 BF16 knee is 989.5 / 3.35 ≈ 295 FLOP/byte; GELU at about 5 remains memory-bound.
A 1024² BF16 matmul has intensity about 341, just beyond the knee, so it reaches the compute-bound plateau.
slides.check: Optimizing FLOP count cannot rescue a bandwidth-bound kernel if it moves the same bytes.
slides.equation: performance = min(3.35 TB/s × I, 989.5 TFLOP/s); knee ≈ 295 FLOP/byte

slides.title: Why training fills an activation shelf
slides.lede: Backward needs intermediate layer outputs, so an ordinary forward pass retains activations that inference can discard after each layer.
beats: In the lecture's simplified BF16 term, activation memory is 2 × B × D × L bytes.
For B=64, D=1024, and L=16, that term is 2,097,152 bytes = 2 MiB.
This is one accounting term, not total peak memory: parameters, gradients, optimizer state, temporary buffers, and framework overhead are separate.
slides.check: If only L doubles while B and D stay fixed, which part of this simplified memory term doubles?
slides.equation: M_activations = 2 bytes × B × D × L = 2 MiB

slides.title: Discard now, rematerialize during backward
slides.lede: Activation checkpointing, gradient checkpointing, and rematerialization name the same core exchange: save a subset of activations and recompute missing ones from the latest saved checkpoint.
beats: The forward pass keeps selected boundaries such as h3, h6, and h9 instead of every intermediate activation.
During backward, the program reruns the needed forward layers inside each interval before computing gradients.
Saved activation memory falls, but the additional forward work means checkpointing is not free.
slides.check: To recover h8 while backpropagating from h9, which saved checkpoint is the natural restart point?

slides.title: Checkpoint placement is a resource schedule
slides.lede: The source closes Lecture 2 by comparing three regimes. Selective placement between the extremes gives a useful memory/compute balance.
beats: Store every layer: O(L) saved activation memory and no recomputation.
Store no layer activations: O(1) saved activation memory but O(L²) recomputation when restarting from the beginning for each layer.
Store every √L layers: O(√L) saved activation memory and O(L) recomputation in the lecture's schedule.
slides.check: For L=16, every √L layers means an interval of four layers; compare the number of saved boundaries with storing all 16.
slides.equation: every layer: [O(L), 0] · none: [O(1), O(L²)] · every √L: [O(√L), O(L)]
